title: Week 1 · Lesson 4: Adaptive Immunity — FNP-Level Approach
html:
PHASE 1 · ADVANCED PATHOPHYSIOLOGY + CLINICAL REASONING

Week 1 — Lesson 4: Adaptive Immunity

FNP-level goal: Use B-cell, T-cell, antibody, and antigen-presentation mechanisms to reason through vaccination, immunosuppression, allergy, autoimmune disease, and infection risk.

Learning Objectives

  • Distinguish humoral from cell-mediated immunity.
  • Explain antigen presentation and the MHC I–CD8 / MHC II–CD4 relationship.
  • Apply immunoglobulin functions to clinical patterns.
  • Differentiate active from passive immunity and primary from secondary response.
  • Recognize anaphylaxis and altered-immunocompetence considerations that change disposition or vaccine planning.

Part 1 — What Adaptive Immunity Adds

Innate immunity responds rapidly to patterns of injury and pathogens. Adaptive immunity is antigen-specific and develops memory. It uses B cells, T cells, antibodies, antigen presentation, clonal expansion, and memory cells.

Antigen exposure → lymphocyte activation and clonal expansion → effector response + memory → faster, stronger response on later exposure.

The FNP question is not simply “Which antibody is this?” It is: Does the patient have an effective immune response, an inappropriate immune response, or a treatment-related loss of protection?

Part 2 — B Cells and Humoral Immunity

B cells recognize antigen and, with appropriate signals, differentiate into plasma cells and memory B cells.

B cell → plasma cell → antibody production.

Antibodies can neutralize pathogens/toxins, opsonize targets, activate complement in appropriate settings, and help prevent reinfection. Memory B cells support an accelerated response after subsequent exposure.

Part 3 — Antibodies: Functional Map

  • IgM: an early major antibody in a primary response. It should not be used alone to date an infection without understanding the specific assay and clinical context.
  • IgG: major systemic long-term antibody; supports neutralization, opsonization, and secondary responses. Maternal IgG crosses the placenta and provides passive fetal/newborn protection.
  • IgA: important at mucosal surfaces and in secretions, including respiratory/GI secretions and breast milk.
  • IgE: binds mast cells/basophils and is central to immediate allergic responses and helminth defense.
  • IgD: has a limited routine clinical role and is associated with B-cell surface function.

FNP reasoning: a laboratory antibody result may reflect prior exposure, vaccination, timing of illness, or assay limitations. Never interpret a serology result outside the clinical question it was ordered to answer.

Part 4 — T Cells and Antigen Presentation

T cells generally respond to processed antigen displayed with MHC molecules.

MHC I → CD8. Most nucleated cells express MHC I. Intracellular peptides, such as viral proteins produced within an infected cell, can be displayed to CD8 cytotoxic T cells.

MHC II → CD4. Professional antigen-presenting cells—dendritic cells, macrophages, and B cells—display extracellularly derived antigen to CD4 helper T cells.

CD4 helper cells coordinate: they provide cytokine and co-stimulatory support to B cells, macrophages, and other lymphocytes.

CD8 cytotoxic cells eliminate: they can kill infected or abnormal target cells that present the relevant antigen on MHC I.

Part 5 — Why MHC Matters Clinically

A viral infection within a host cell creates an intracellular-antigen problem: MHC I presentation and CD8 activity are central. A phagocyte processing extracellular bacterial material creates an MHC II/CD4 coordination problem.

This framework also explains why impaired T-cell function can increase susceptibility to opportunistic infection and why B-cell–directed therapy can blunt antibody responses. It does not replace individual risk assessment, medication review, or specialist input.

Part 6 — Primary, Secondary, Active, and Passive Immunity

A primary response takes time to develop. On re-exposure, memory B and T cells allow a faster and stronger secondary response.

Active immunity: the patient’s immune system produces the response after vaccination or infection; memory can develop.

Passive immunity: antibodies come from another source, such as maternal transfer or administered immunoglobulin. Protection is immediate but temporary and does not create the same recipient memory.

Vaccination leverages adaptive memory. Vaccine selection, timing, and expected response depend on age, conditions, medications, prior doses, pregnancy status, and current public-health guidance.

Part 7 — Allergy and Anaphylaxis

In an immediate IgE-mediated reaction, allergen cross-linking on mast cells/basophils triggers mediator release.

IgE-mediated mast-cell activation → vasodilation + permeability ↑ + bronchoconstriction + mucosal edema.

Clinical manifestations can include urticaria, angioedema, wheeze, throat tightness, hypotension, syncope, vomiting, or rapidly progressive symptoms.

Anaphylaxis is an emergency. Airway, breathing, circulation, rapid emergency treatment, and emergency transfer take priority; do not delay escalation while waiting for rash progression or a laboratory test.

Part 8 — Loss of Tolerance: Autoimmunity

Adaptive immunity is harmful when tolerance to self is lost. Autoimmune disease can be predominantly antibody-mediated, T-cell–mediated, or mixed. The FNP task is to connect the pattern—such as inflammatory arthritis, rash, cytopenias, endocrine dysfunction, renal findings, or neuropathy—to a focused differential and timely evaluation.

Do not diagnose systemic autoimmune disease from a screening antibody alone. Results must be interpreted with symptoms, examination, objective organ involvement, pretest probability, and when appropriate, specialty collaboration.

Part 9 — Immunosuppression and Vaccination

Medications and conditions that alter immune competence can increase infection risk and reduce vaccine response. Examples include chemotherapy, transplant-related immunosuppression, advanced HIV, high-dose systemic corticosteroids, and selected biologic/anti-B-cell therapies.

FNP practice requires complete medication reconciliation and up-to-date vaccine guidance. Non-live vaccines are generally safe in altered immunocompetence, although effectiveness may be reduced. Live-vaccine suitability and timing can differ substantially by immune status and therapy; verify current guidance and coordinate with the treating specialist rather than relying on a one-size-fits-all rule.

Part 10 — Diagnostics: Match Test to Question

Examples: CBC with differential for cytopenia patterns; HIV testing when clinically indicated; quantitative immunoglobulins in selected recurrent/unusual infection patterns; targeted serology when it changes management; and source-directed testing for suspected infection.

Ask: Am I evaluating acute infection, immunity after prior exposure/vaccination, autoimmune disease, medication-related immune suppression, or a dangerous allergic event?

Part 11 — FNP Disposition

Emergency: suspected anaphylaxis, airway swelling, wheezing/respiratory distress, hypotension/syncope after possible allergen exposure, or severe infection in an immunocompromised patient.

Expedited evaluation: recurrent unusual/opportunistic infections, unexplained severe cytopenias, suspected systemic autoimmune organ involvement, or a patient receiving immunosuppressive therapy with significant infectious symptoms.

Part 12 — Board-Style Case 1

A patient develops hives, wheeze, throat tightness, vomiting, and lightheadedness minutes after a medication exposure.

Mechanism: likely immediate hypersensitivity with IgE-mediated mast-cell activation causing bronchoconstriction, edema, and circulatory compromise.

FNP decision: treat as anaphylaxis and arrange emergency management; do not observe in routine clinic while waiting to see whether symptoms resolve.

Part 13 — Board-Style Case 2

A patient receiving anti-B-cell therapy asks whether a needed vaccine will work normally.

Think: B-cell-directed therapy can reduce antibody production. Confirm the medication, timing, vaccine type, indication, and current guidance; coordinate the plan with the relevant treating clinician rather than making an unsupported universal statement.

FNP High-Yield Framework

B cell → plasma cell → antibody; memory B cell → faster later response.

MHC I → CD8 → intracellular-antigen target-cell killing.

MHC II → CD4 → coordination and B-cell/macrophage help.

IgG systemic/placental; IgA mucosal; IgE immediate allergy; IgM early primary response.

FNP decision: identify immune mechanism, assess host risk and instability, use testing purposefully, and escalate immediately for anaphylaxis or serious infection.
